newsitem.title: HAITI: Unsafe Haitian boats to be blocked from U.S. ports.
newsitem.headline: Unsafe Haitian boats to be blocked from U.S. ports.

text.p: New rules barring small vessels deemed unseaworthy by the U.S. Coast Guard from U.S. ports have angered Haitian officials, who say most of their country's fleet will be left high and dry.
Officials from both sides will meet in Miami on Friday to discuss a possible easing of the new safety standards, due to come into effect in July.

The provision, called Operation Safety Net, covers all vessels under 500 tonnes arriving in U.S. ports. It ensures they are safe to sail in international waters. Unseaworthy boats are liable to be seized and the crew arrested.

Small Haitian boats, especially the rickety wooden craft originally designed for fishing, have a reputation for being unsafe, said U.S. Coast Guard Commander William Uberti, chief of the standards enforcement department.
"They are dangerous, overloaded, they often run aground and capsize," he said in an interview from Miami. "We have to rescue them about once a month."
Haiti's port director, Duquepson Extra, said most of the country's small vessel fleet would be hit.
"This provision will have the impact of closing all of Haiti's ports, except for the capital. The majority of boats, 34 out of 36 of them, will be blocked," Extra said.
Haitian port officials said the new law had more to do with U.S. concern about drug trafficking in the Caribbean than about the safety of Haitian merchants.

U.S. law enforcement officials say the Caribbean is the new bridge for cocaine trafficking between Colombia and Florida. Haiti, with its proximity to the United States and ill-equipped police force, is considered a potential weak link in U.S. efforts to stop the flow of drugs.

Haiti has so far declined to sign a drug interdiction treaty with the United States which would allow the U.S. Coast Guard to pursue a ship into the national waters of any Caribbean nation that signs on.
Under Operation Safety Net, the U.S. Coast Guard would be able to board all small vessels to check their structure.
"Of course, at the same time you are doing an inspection, you can look for drugs," said one Haitian port officer.

Petty Officer Scott Carr of the U.S. Coast Guard in Miami said the Coast Guard did not have the authority to board boats in international waters without permission from the national governments. Inspections for seaworthiness would take place in U.S. waters or ports, where agents were already empowered to mount searches for drugs and contraband if they wanted to.
"The idea is to keep sub-standard vessels out of U.S. ports. It's not just Haitian vessels," he said.

Extra said the law would devastate the Haitian export sector. If the provincial ports were to close, exporters would be forced to move their products, often agriculatural exports, over poor and often non-existant roads to the capital.
"We are willing to ensure our boats have life jackets, radios and other safety equipment but there is not such a problem with these boats to block them off completely," he said.
